title: Geometric Dimensioning & Tolerancing (GD&T)
summary: The GD&T language for defining and controlling form, orientation, location, profile, and runout using datums and feature control frames.

sections.heading: Why GD&T Beats Coordinate Tolerancing
sections.content:
Conventional (coordinate) dimensioning places a tolerance on each linear dimension independently, creating a square tolerance zone and leaving form, orientation, and datums implicit. **Geometric Dimensioning & Tolerancing (GD&T)** instead uses a precise symbolic language to define *functional* tolerance zones with clear datums, so a hole's location is controlled by a cylindrical zone rather than an ambiguous square.

GD&T answers three questions a coordinate drawing cannot:
1. **What is the tolerance zone shape?** (cylinder, plane, surface, profile)
2. **What is it referenced to?** (a datum reference frame)
3. **Can the tolerance grow when the part departs from MMC?** (bonus tolerance)

sections.heading: Datum Reference Frames (DRF)
sections.content:
A **datum** is a theoretically exact plane, axis, or point established from a *datum feature* (the physical surface on the part). The **Datum Reference Frame** is the coordinate system the tolerances are measured from, built using the **3-2-1 rule**:

- **Primary datum** — contacts at least 3 points (a plane)
- **Secondary datum** — contacts at least 2 points (aligns one axis)
- **Tertiary datum** — contacts at least 1 point (locks rotation)

In a feature control frame, datums appear in order of precedence, e.g. `A | B | C`. Always prefer datums on **functional surfaces** — mating faces, bearing seats, or locating features — never on surfaces that carry no assembly relationship.

sections.heading: Anatomy of a Feature Control Frame
sections.content:
The **feature control frame** is the heart of GD&T. Reading it left to right:

| Compartment | Contents | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Geometric characteristic symbol | ⌀ position (⌖) |
| 2 | Total tolerance value + diameter modifier | `⌀ 0.1` |
| 3 | Material condition modifier | `M` (MMC), `L` (LMC), blank (RFS) |
| 4+ | Datum references in precedence order | `A │ B │ C` |

A typical control for a bolt-hole pattern reads:

`⌖  ⌀0.1(M)  A  B  C`

meaning: the hole axis must lie inside a `⌀0.1` cylindrical tolerance zone, located from datum frame A-B-C, evaluated at Maximum Material Condition (so the zone can grow by the bonus tolerance).

sections.heading: The Five Tolerance Categories
sections.content:
All 14 GD&T symbols (ASME Y14.5) fall into five functional groups:

| Category | Symbols | What it controls |
|---|---|---|
| **Form** | Straightness, Flatness, Circularity, Cylindricity | Shape of a feature alone, no datums |
| **Orientation** | Perpendicularity, Angularity, Parallelism | Angle of a feature relative to a datum |
| **Location** | Position, Concentricity, Symmetry | Placement of features relative to datums |
| **Profile** | Profile of a line, Profile of a surface | Outline or surface in 2D / 3D |
| **Runout** | Circular runout, Total runout | Composite deviation of a surface of revolution |

**Design guidance:** location and orientation controls are referenced to datums; form controls (flatness, straightness) are *independent* — they apply within the size tolerance and do not reference datums.

sections.heading: MMC, LMC & Bonus Tolerance
sections.content:
Material condition modifiers let a tolerance **grow** when the feature departs from its worst-case size:

- **Maximum Material Condition (MMC)** — the size at which the feature holds the most material: the smallest hole / largest pin.
- **Least Material Condition (LMC)** — the size at which the feature holds the least material: the largest hole / smallest pin.
- **Regardless of Feature Size (RFS)** — no modifier; the tolerance does not change with size.

For a hole callout `⌀0.1(M)` with a `⌀10.0` MMC size: if the machined hole measures `⌀10.15`, the **bonus tolerance** is:

$$T_{bonus} = D_{actual} - D_{MMC} = 10.15 - 10.00 = 0.15 \text{ mm}$$

The **total allowable position tolerance** becomes $0.1 + 0.15 = 0.25$ mm — exactly why GD&T is more economical than a fixed coordinate tolerance: it rewards features that naturally arrive at less-critical sizes.

sections.heading: GD&T in the Manufacturing Loop
sections.content:
GD&T is not just a drawing language — it drives **inspection**. A coordinate measuring machine (CMM) or optical comparator evaluates features against the feature control frame, applying the same MMC bonus logic the designer intended.

Practical rules for the design loop:
- Apply GD&T to **functional interfaces only** — over-tolerancing inflates cost.
- Reference **machined datum features**, not raw cast surfaces.
- Use the fixed-fastener rule $T \geq H - F$ when sizing clearance holes for bolt patterns.
- Pass GD&T data into [[cad-computer-aided-design|CAD drawings]], verify fit in CAE assembly analysis, and communicate critical features to [[machining-fundamentals|machining]] and inspection.

keyTakeaways: GD&T replaces ambiguous square coordinate zones with functional cylindrical or planar tolerance zones.
A Datum Reference Frame (3-2-1 rule) is required for orientation, location, profile, and runout controls.
MMC modifiers award bonus tolerance when the feature departs from its maximum-material size.
The fixed fastener rule T ≥ H - F is the quickest way to size clearance-hole patterns.
Always evaluate GD&T callouts at inspection time using the same logic the designer specified.
